profiles.name: Rye Billsbury
profiles.excerpt: Rye Billsbury was a working announcer and character actor whose microphone career connected mystery, comedy and anthology radio across the 1940s and 1950s.
profiles.bio_html:
Rye Billsbury is better preserved through broadcast credits than through conventional biographical publicity. Golden Radio Hour’s detailed people data shows him repeatedly in announcing work, especially on Mystery House, while also appearing as a performer on mystery, comedy and anthology programs.

That combination was common in network radio but still required two distinct skills. The announcer had to handle sponsor material, openings and transitions with absolute clarity, while the actor had to disappear into character once the drama began. Billsbury’s record moves between those functions rather than fitting a single star role.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 27 Mystery House announcer credits, six Abbott and Costello Show announcing credits, two Duffy’s Tavern announcing credits and additional acting appearances on The Whistler, Lux Radio Theatre, Tales of the Texas Rangers and other programs. GRH keeps the profile centered on that documented radio career rather than inventing details the surviving sources do not support.

profiles.name: Ralph Camargo
profiles.excerpt: Ralph Camargo moved between stage acting, radio repertory and narration, using the same disciplined voice that later made him a familiar industrial-film narrator.
profiles.bio_html:
Ralph Camargo built his career primarily as a stage actor, but radio and narration became important parallel crafts. Born in 1912, he worked in theatre and in daytime radio, including Guiding Light, before continuing into television and film.

Camargo’s voice also became familiar outside conventional drama through narration for industrial and promotional films. That background helps explain his recurring use as narrator in later radio anthologies, where a narrator had to establish tone quickly and carry exposition without flattening the drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 Theater Five narrator/performer credits, four CBS Radio Workshop narration credits and additional performances on X Minus One, Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, Dimension X and other series. His page therefore treats narration as a real secondary radio profession rather than as an incidental label.

profiles.name: Phillip Clarke
profiles.excerpt: Phillip Clarke served as the ominous host of The Sealed Book while also working as a repertory actor in mystery and dramatic radio.
profiles.bio_html:
Phillip Clarke is most clearly preserved in radio history as the host of The Sealed Book, the 1945 mystery anthology built around macabre stories introduced by a recurring book-and-key framing device. The host’s job was not simply to announce a title. He established the ritual and atmosphere that made separate stories feel like parts of the same series.

Clarke also worked as an actor on other dramatic programs, including Mr. Keen, Tracer of Lost Persons, The Mysterious Traveler and literary anthologies. That repertory work gave him a broader radio identity than the Sealed Book opening alone suggests.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 24 Sealed Book host credits, 12 Mr. Keen performances and additional appearances on The Mysterious Traveler, Words at War, Columbia Workshop and Matinee Theater. GRH therefore classifies him as both actor and host.

profiles.name: Ray Collins
profiles.excerpt: Ray Collins was one of Orson Welles’s essential radio repertory actors, using narration and character work to help define the Mercury Theatre before becoming familiar to television audiences as Lieutenant Tragg.
profiles.bio_html:
Ray Collins had already spent decades on stage and radio before television made him widely recognizable as Lieutenant Arthur Tragg on Perry Mason. Born in Sacramento in 1889, he began acting as a teenager and became part of the elite New York radio repertory world of the 1930s.

His association with Orson Welles began before the Mercury Theatre and became central to both men’s careers. Collins worked on The Shadow, Les Misérables, The Mercury Theatre on the Air and The Campbell Playhouse, shifting between leads, supporting roles and narration. In the famous War of the Worlds broadcast, he played multiple parts, including the rooftop reporter describing New York’s destruction.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 16 Mercury Theatre on the Air narrator/performer credits, nine Columbia Workshop narrator/performer credits and seven Shadow performances. His biography treats narration as part of the repertory craft that made him one of Welles’s most trusted radio actors.

profiles.name: Kenny Delmar
profiles.excerpt: Kenny Delmar was Fred Allen’s announcer and the creator of Senator Claghorn, proving how easily a radio announcer could become one of the show’s biggest comic characters.
profiles.bio_html:
Kenny Delmar entered entertainment as a child performer and found his durable career in radio announcing and character work. By the late 1930s he was announcing major programs such as The March of Time and appearing in dramatic radio, including Orson Welles’s Mercury productions.

His defining success came on The Fred Allen Show. Delmar served as the regular announcer while also creating Senator Beauregard Claghorn, the booming Southern politician of Allen’s Alley. The character became a national catchphrase phenomenon and later influenced Warner Bros.’ Foghorn Leghorn. What made the bit especially effective was the contrast between Delmar’s smooth announcer voice and the exaggerated Claghorn persona.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 72 Fred Allen Show announcer/performer credits, 44 Shadow performances and additional Mercury, Columbia Workshop and anthology work. His page therefore places announcing and acting together, exactly as listeners experienced them.

profiles.name: Joe DeSantis
profiles.excerpt: Joe DeSantis brought a multilingual New York actor’s authority to radio repertory and to landmark narration such as Norman Corwin’s On a Note of Triumph.
profiles.bio_html:
Joseph DeSantis was born in New York City in 1909 to Italian immigrant parents and began broadcasting in Italian-language radio before building a wider career in English-language drama. He studied sculpture and drama at New York University and worked with the WPA during the Depression, bringing both artistic training and lived immigrant experience into a long acting career.

Radio used DeSantis for a broad range of characters, but narration was also central to his reputation. One of his most important assignments was Norman Corwin’s On a Note of Triumph, the nationwide broadcast marking the end of the war in Europe. His resonant, serious delivery made him especially effective in documentary and literary radio as well as crime and science-fiction drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 21 Suspense performances, 16 X Minus One, eight Words at War, seven Columbia Workshop narrator/performer credits and additional anthology work. GRH therefore preserves narration as a significant part of his radio craft.

profiles.name: Alan Devitt
profiles.excerpt: Alan Devitt was a flexible New York radio actor who could move from Shadow character parts into announcing duties without leaving the repertory company around him.
profiles.bio_html:
Alan Devitt is best documented through the cast records of New York dramatic radio. He worked repeatedly on The Shadow during the Orson Welles era, taking multiple supporting parts and, on some broadcasts, handling announcing duties as well.

That combination is revealing. Dramatic radio often depended on repertory performers who could double several characters, cover continuity and adapt to whatever a live script required. Devitt’s credits show exactly that kind of flexibility rather than a career built around one famous signature role.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 16 Shadow announcer/performer credits, 11 Inner Sanctum Mysteries performances and a Words at War appearance. GRH keeps his page grounded in those verified broadcasts because reliable personal-life documentation remains limited.

profiles.name: Carl Frank
profiles.excerpt: Carl Frank combined repertory acting with the formal announcing voice of This Is Your FBI, helping give the government-backed crime series its official public-service tone.
profiles.bio_html:
Carl Frank worked in dramatic radio as both actor and announcer. His acting credits include the Welles-era Shadow and Mercury Theatre productions, but his clearest sustained announcing assignment was This Is Your FBI, the ABC crime series produced with official FBI cooperation.

On that program the announcer did more than identify the sponsor. The opening and closing language framed dramatized cases as public service and institutional authority, connecting the Equitable Life Assurance Society’s sponsorship with the FBI’s own desired public image. Frank’s controlled delivery helped establish that official tone during the program’s early eastern broadcasts.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 24 This Is Your FBI announcer credits, seven Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances and additional work on The Shadow, The Mercury Theatre on the Air, Dr. Christian and X Minus One. GRH therefore treats announcing as a substantial second profession in his radio record.

profiles.name: John Griggs
profiles.excerpt: John Griggs was a New York radio repertory actor whose work in Columbia Workshop and Words at War also placed him in narration-heavy experimental and documentary drama.
profiles.bio_html:
John Griggs appears in the surviving radio record as a working New York repertory actor rather than a personality built around one long-running series. He participated in programs such as Columbia Workshop, where experimental writing and sound often required actors to move between character and narrative functions.

The Workshop’s production records place Griggs in Norman Corwin material such as You Can Dream, Inc., while GRH also preserves work on Words at War, Theater Five, 2000 Plus, X Minus One and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar. The narration tags on Columbia productions are consistent with that broader repertory use.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves six Words at War performances, five Theater Five appearances, three Columbia Workshop narrator/performer credits and smaller science-fiction and detective roles. Personal documentation remains limited, so GRH centers the profile on the programs themselves.
